newsitem.title: CHINA: Metals industry ponders China zinc sales.
newsitem.headline: Metals industry ponders China zinc sales.

text.p: Just why China sold hundreds of thousands of tonnes of zinc it did not have at bargain basement prices in the midst of a bull market has metals traders and industry analysts scratching their heads.
Was it part of a stunning strategy aimed at locking in long-term profits -- a move so obscurely clever that no one noticed it or could understand it?
Or did Chinese metals industry gurus just misjudge the market so badly -- betting the price would go down when the rest of the world seemed to know it would rise?
"How did they read the market so wrong?" a metals industry analyst in Hong Kong asked of the Chinese.
"It is surprising because historically they have been good at reading the market, often even running the market," he said.

China's metals traders have been cheered by recent reversals in world zinc prices, after rises of more than 60 percent since the start of this year caught them short and it looked like it would cost them as much as $100 million.

But contracts for zinc to be delivered in mid-September were still outstanding and could cause the market to rise against them again as the delivery dates near, Chinese and Western trading sources said.
China is a major factor in the trading of many commodities, from soybeans and sugar to wheat and wolframite and many of the base metals traded on the London Metal Exchange (LME).

China's swing influence is so great that the mere whisper that the country of 1.2 billion people and nearly 10 percent annual economic growth plans to buy or sell can have a dramatic effect on price movements.
Its trading strategy is secretive, statistics generally unreliable and its markets opaque, all adding to China's mystery as a market factor.
When it comes to grains, vegetable oils and other so-called soft commodities, the Chinese have become savvy buyers, waiting for market dips and swooping in to buy in quantity.
So when rumours turned to reality and the extent of losses China faced on the LME became known last week, jaws dropped.
"Has it been a misjudgment or has there been something more Machiavellian in what transpired," one industry analyst said.
"Was it an attempt to manipulate and use the market for their own ends so they could push prices up and buy options to lock in prices for their 1998 production?" he said.
"Though that still wouldn't account for the losses they're now facing -- and it certainly would cover them," he said.

Chinese zinc producers, on the advice of the China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC), the state-run corporation that controls the metals industry, sold about 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes of zinc for around $1,100 a tonne, Chinese industry sources said.

The decision to sell at that price was made late last year, when LME zinc was already around $1,000 a tonne, and when market fundamentals -- tight supply, rising demand -- indicated a rise in the first half of 1997 to at least $1,400-1,450 a tonne.

The offers, which came to more than China could produce, were snapped up, and anyone with any zinc held onto their metal because they knew China would eventually have to come onto the market and buy metal to cover their contracts.
It was the perfect recipe for sky-high prices. By last Monday, zinc was around seven-year highs of $1,700 a tonne and China was facing losses of around $100 million.

On Tuesday, a sell-off led by speculative investment funds triggered a tumble. The price fell $170 a tonne in the first half-hour of trading, and by Wednesday was sitting at $1,460 a tonne. Friday's closing LME cash price was 1,559.
One source at a smelter with 90,000 tonnes of forward contracts to cover quipped that the falls would at least cut his smelter's losses.

Meetings being held at the upper echelons of CNNC, which is administered by the State Council, or cabinet, could last weeks as leaders grapple with what went wrong and decide how to deal with it, CNNC sources have said.
The situation has highlighted the lack of independence the industry has, with factories taking direction from above, the analysts said.

While one analyst in Hong Kong suggested it could lead to wariness on the part of foreigners wanting to do business with China, most others polled by Reuters said the industry was just shaking its head and accepting China had made a mistake.
"Hopefully, they will learn from the mistake," said an Australian analyst.
"It's a pity they got caught so badly, but you can't blame anyone for taking advantage of them, that's what it's all about. Maybe next time it will be their turn to win," he said.
